references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus asks the disciples the same question: "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?"
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus asks the disciples: "Who do people say that I am?" This is the closest parallel to Luke's account.
Luke emphasizes Jesus' prayer life. Here Jesus withdraws to pray, just as he does in Luke 9:18 before asking the decisive question of the disciples.
Jesus prays alone before an important moment – here before choosing the twelve apostles. The same pattern is seen in Luke 9:18, where prayer precedes the decisive question about his identity.
Another example of Jesus' prayer practice in the Gospel of Luke, showing that Luke places special emphasis on Jesus praying at important occasions.
Herod asks exactly the same question that Jesus now poses to the disciples: "Who is this?" The popular answers (John, Elijah, one of the prophets) are the same in both texts.
The disciples' answer to Jesus' question, where they report public opinion and Peter confesses Jesus as God's Messiah. This is the direct continuation of verse 18.
Herod's and the people's speculations about Jesus' identity – whether he is John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets – are directly reflected in the question Jesus asks in Luke 9:18.

Jesus' prayer at his baptism in the Jordan, where his identity as God's Son is revealed. Prayer and revelation of identity are linked together, just as in 9:18 where prayer is followed by the question of who Jesus is.
